prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

For instance, one participant expressed their priorities clearly: “I just want safe and protected bike lanes, safe pedestrian crossings, wider and shaded footpaths, and raised crossings at intersections, so cars have to go over the raised area instead of pedestrians having to go down onto the road” (M, 36). The need for broader changes to address these issues was repeatedly highlighted, as another participant noted: “Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, there are not enough safe crossings with islands, cyclists should always have permanent, dedicated lanes wherever there is a road, and they should really fix the train bridges so there are no at-road level crossings. More pedestrian refuge islands is also a brilliant opportunity to plant more trees” (F, 31). These suggestions underline the interconnected benefits of safety improvements and environmental enhancements. Participants consistently linked infrastructure upgrades to safety and justice, reflecting a belief that physical changes to the transport system are foundational for achieving equity. One participant succinctly summarised this perspective: “The government desperately needs to improve the pedestrian and cyclist safety situations. Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, and there are not enough safe crossings with islands” (F, 33). Another added, “Prioritise infrastructure for vulnerable road users so we don’t have to share with any motor vehicles” (M, 52). Many criticised proposals requiring VRUs to use reflective clothing, specific apps, or wearable devices to ensure their visibility to CAVs. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)

Selected Indicators:

 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

For instance, one participant expressed their priorities clearly: “I just want safe and protected bike lanes, safe pedestrian crossings, wider and shaded footpaths, and raised crossings at intersections, so cars have to go over the raised area instead of pedestrians having to go down onto the road” (M, 36). The need for broader changes to address these issues was repeatedly highlighted, as another participant noted: “Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, there are not enough safe crossings with islands, cyclists should always have permanent, dedicated lanes wherever there is a road, and they should really fix the train bridges so there are no at-road level crossings. More pedestrian refuge islands is also a brilliant opportunity to plant more trees” (F, 31). These suggestions underline the interconnected benefits of safety improvements and environmental enhancements. Participants consistently linked infrastructure upgrades to safety and justice, reflecting a belief that physical changes to the transport system are foundational for achieving equity. One participant succinctly summarised this perspective: “The government desperately needs to improve the pedestrian and cyclist safety situations. Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, and there are not enough safe crossings with islands” (F, 33). Another added, “Prioritise infrastructure for vulnerable road users so we don’t have to share with any motor vehicles” (M, 52). Collectively, these responses reflect a strong consensus that redesigning infrastructure is essential for creating a safer and fairer transport system that can effectively integrate CAVs. 3.5.3. Inclusivity and accessibility Codes such as “inclusive design,” “accessible vehicles,” and “no burden on VRUs” reflected participants’ concerns about marginalised groups, particularly people with disabilities, the elderly, and those without access to wearable technology. Concerns around inclusivity and accessibility were prominent, with participants firmly rejecting policies that placed the burden of adaptation on VRUs. Many criticised proposals requiring VRUs to use reflective clothing, specific apps, or wearable devices to ensure their visibility to CAVs. One participant voiced their frustration: “Pedestrians should NOT have to wear something so that these cars can see them… If the robot can’t see pedestrians, then it should not be allowed on the road” (NB, 18). Another participant echoed this sentiment: “There is no way you can insist that all people walking around roads must have a smartphone with a specific app or wear hi-vis clothing; that is silly. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority. Intersections with a high proportion of large vehicles should be equipped with right-turn protection islands to remind non-motor vehicles and pedestrians and prevent motor vehicles turning right from encroaching on the left-turn waiting space of non-motor vehicles, thereby ensuring non-motor vehicle safety. Where there is substantial mid-block crossing demand, such as along sections adjacent to schools, shopping malls, transit hubs, exhibition halls, nursing homes, etc., and where the spacing between adjacent intersections is relatively large (>500 m), or where there are no other crossing facilities (pedestrian overpasses or underpasses), pedestrian crosswalk markings shall be provided in conjunction with directional signs, and pedestrian signal lights shall be installed as appropriate. B. On road sections with three or more lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or where the peak-hour two-way motor vehicle flow exceeds 750 pcu and the 12-hour flow exceeds 8000 pcu, pedestrian signal lights shall be installed when the peak-hour pedestrian flow crossing the crosswalk exceeds 500 persons. Where the above conditions are not met but the design speed of the road section exceeds 50 km/h, push-button pedestrian signal lights shall be installed. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Pedestrian crosswalks and related facilities shall be arranged as far as possible in accordance with the principle of the shortest pedestrian crossing route. B. No on-street parking bays or bus stops shall be located within 9 m upstream or downstream of a pedestrian crosswalk. In principle, pedestrian crosswalks shall be set at the rear end of bus stops and shall avoid bus stopping areas. C.
